abstract: Background Generative AI chatbots are increasingly used for mental health–related purposes, yet little is known about the factors associated with such use or AI chatbot dependence. Objective This study examined factors associated with young adults’ use of AI chatbots for emotional self-disclosure and mental health–related support, as well as the associations between AI chatbot use and dependence. Methods A cross-sectional online survey of individuals aged 18 to 29 years was conducted in Japan. Self-report measures assessed psychosocial factors (self-esteem and loneliness), mental health symptoms (anxiety and depression), AI chatbot use (emotional self-disclosure and mental health–related support), and AI chatbot dependence (emotional dependence and social anxiety–related dependence). Results Of 820 participants, 381 (46.5%) reported using AI chatbots for emotional self-disclosure at least once in the past month, including 65 (7.9%) who reported doing so every day or almost every day. In addition, 336 (41%) reported using AI chatbots for mental health–related support, including 53 (6.5%) who reported doing so every day or almost every day. Anxiety and depressive symptoms were combined into a composite measure of mental health symptoms because they are highly correlated. Multivariable logistic regression showed that greater mental health symptom severity, but not self-esteem or loneliness, was associated with both emotional self-disclosure (odds ratio [OR] 2.23, 95% CI 1.85-2.69; P<.001) and mental health–related support (OR 2.42, 95% CI 2.01-2.94; P<.001). Among emotional self-disclosure users (n=381), the frequency of emotional self-disclosure was positively associated with emotional dependence (β=0.334; P<.001) and social anxiety–related dependence (β=0.307; P<.001). Path analyses indicated that a model specifying psychosocial factors and mental health symptoms as antecedent variables to AI chatbot use and dependence fit the data better than an alternative model specifying AI chatbot use and dependence as the antecedent variables (comparative fit index [CFI]=0.994 vs 0.583; root mean square error of approximation [RMSEA]=0.033 vs 0.293). In this model, lower self-esteem and greater loneliness were associated with more severe mental health symptoms, which, in turn, were associated with greater AI chatbot dependence, primarily through direct pathways and, to a lesser extent, through more frequent emotional self-disclosure. Among emotional self-disclosure users, loneliness was the only significant psychosocial correlate of emotional dependence (F1,369=7.78; P=.006). Conclusions Emotional engagement with AI chatbots was common in this sample of young adults in Japan. Findings suggest that young adults experiencing mental health symptoms may be more likely to use AI chatbots for emotional self-disclosure and mental health–related support, while loneliness may be particularly relevant to emotional dependence among users. These findings highlight the need to understand AI chatbot use not only as a technological behavior but also as part of young adults’ broader emotional and help-seeking landscape.

title: Psychosocial Correlates of AI Chatbot Use for Emotional Support Among Young Adults: Cross-Sectional Study
